flags.reason: The question does not say how much of the trial-and-error process is expected, so a one-line answer and a full worked trace would both look defensible to a marker.
flags.evidence: How will you solve it using trial and error method?
flags.rewrite: A jigsaw puzzle has 12 pieces and no reference picture. Describe the trial-and-error process you would follow, listing at least three failed placements and explaining how you decide which piece to try next. (3 marks)

flags.reason: The input "1234 5" contains a space, so "numeric" could mean the whole string, either token, or the string after stripping, and the three readings give different code.
flags.rewrite: Given the string s = "1234 5", write a Python snippet that reports whether s consists only of digits, and state what your snippet prints for s. Name the string method you use. (3 marks)

flags.reason: A flowchart for the first n Fibonacci numbers is undefined at the start: the question does not say whether 0 and 1 both appear, nor what happens for n = 1.
flags.evidence: generate the first 'n' numbers in the Fibonacci sequence
flags.rewrite: Draw a flowchart that prints the first n Fibonacci numbers, starting from 0 and 1, for any integer n >= 1. Include the decision for the case n = 1 and label the loop's exit condition. (3 marks)

flags.reason: Three separate outputs are asked for, including an operator-precedence expression, and each needs a trace worth more than the single mark this sub-question can carry.
flags.rewrite: Write the output produced by each of the following, and for (iii) show the order in which the operators are evaluated. (i) for count in range(-10,-20,-2): print(count, end=" ") (ii) for i in range(10,-1,-2): print(i) (iii) 2*3**2**2 (3 marks)

flags.reason: "N given numbers" never says where the numbers come from or whether negatives count as even, so a correct program can still be marked wrong.
flags.evidence: sum of even numbers from N given numbers
flags.rewrite: Write a Python program that reads N, then reads N integers, and prints the sum of those that are even. Treat 0 as even and negative even numbers as even. Show the output for the input 4, then 3 -2 0 7. (3 marks)

flags.reason: "Motivation" has no stated scope, so answers range from one sentence to a page and markers have no anchor.
flags.evidence: What is the motivation for using a randomized approach
flags.rewrite: State two reasons why a randomized approach is preferred over a deterministic one for a problem where the input distribution is unknown, and give one example problem where randomization helps. (3 marks)

flags.reason: A brute-force recovery of a 4-digit password is asked for without any constraint on the search space or attempt limit, so "an algorithm" could be 10,000 attempts or a single guess.
flags.evidence: Write an algorithm for recovering the 4-digit numeric password
flags.rewrite: A 4-digit numeric password is verified by a function check(p) that returns true only for the correct password. Write an algorithm that recovers the password by exhaustive search over all 4-digit strings, and state the maximum number of calls to check it makes. (3 marks)

flags.reason: Part a) asks for the backtracking strategy and its application to Sudoku, which are two separate answers, and the 5 marks do not say how they are split.
flags.evidence: Explain how backtracking strategy can be applied to solve Sudoku problem?
flags.rewrite: a) State the backtracking strategy in two or three sentences, then apply it to a 4x4 Sudoku by showing the state after the first two placements and the first point at which the algorithm backtracks. (5 marks)

flags.reason: "Apply Means-Ends Analysis to develop the software" has no stated goal state or operators, which are the two things the technique is defined by, so any narrative answer is acceptable.
flags.evidence: How will you apply Means-Ends Analysis to develop the software?
flags.rewrite: Apply Means-Ends Analysis to the goal "a campus management system where a student can register for a course". State the current state, the goal state, two operators, and the difference each operator reduces. (6 marks)

flags.reason: The grade bands overlap (60-70 and 50-69 both include neither 60 nor 69 cleanly against 70-79), and the "next multiple of 10" rule has no tie-break, so two correct pseudocodes can grade the same mark differently.
flags.evidence: Marks 60-70: Grade D; Marks 50-69: Grade E
flags.rewrite: Write pseudocode for a grading system using these bands: 90-100 A, 80-89 B, 70-79 C, 60-69 D, 50-59 E, below 50 F. Then apply this promotion rule: if the mark is within 3 below the next multiple of 10, raise it to the next band, except when the mark is below 50. Handle exactly 50 and exactly 90 explicitly. (6 marks)

flags.reason: Part b) describes a long logistics scenario but the actual task, printing numbers divisible by 6 and not by 4, is a two-line loop that is worth less than the 3 marks it carries.
flags.evidence: divisible by 6 ... but not divisible by 4
flags.rewrite: b) Write an algorithm that reads a list of n delivery times and prints only those divisible by 6 but not by 4. Then state the time complexity of your algorithm and justify it. (3 marks)

flags.reason: "Ensuring the solution is efficient for real-world applications" is not a measurable requirement, so efficiency cannot be marked either way.
flags.evidence: ensuring the solution is efficient for real-world applications
flags.rewrite: a) Write the pseudocode to find the largest and smallest numbers in a list of N numbers. State the number of comparisons your solution makes in the worst case, and explain why a single pass is or is not sufficient. (6 marks)

flags.reason: Part b) does not state the tolerance for the right-triangle test, which matters for floating-point side lengths and for whether the sides are integers.
flags.evidence: determine whether or not the triangle is a right triangle
flags.rewrite: b) Write a program that reads the three side lengths of a triangle as floating-point numbers and decides whether it is right-angled, using a tolerance of 1e-9 when comparing a^2 + b^2 with c^2. Also report whether the three sides form a valid triangle at all. (4 marks)

flags.reason: Part b) asks for a classification rule, a rearrangement, and a single-word output, which is three asks inside 3 marks.
flags.evidence: all capital letters to appear first, followed by small letters, then digits, and finally any special characters
flags.rewrite: b) Write a Python function that takes a string and returns its characters rearranged as capitals, then small letters, then digits, then other characters, preserving the order within each group. Show the result for "Py3_th@on". (3 marks)

flags.reason: The question asks for a Divide and Conquer solution but the paper gives no array to work on, so the "suitable example" is entirely of the candidate’s choosing.
flags.rewrite: a) Given the array of loan interest rates [9.5, 7.25, 11.0, 8.4, 6.9, 10.2], find the sum of the two smallest rates using a Divide and Conquer approach. Show the split, the combine step, and the recurrence for the running time. (6 marks)

flags.reason: The greedy task-scheduling problem never says whether tasks must be taken in the given order or may be sorted, and the two readings have different answers.
flags.evidence: maximum number of tasks you can complete in a given total time limit
flags.rewrite: b) Given an array of task durations and a total time limit T, determine the maximum number of tasks that can be completed. State whether tasks may be reordered; if they may, sort by duration ascending and justify why that greedy choice is optimal. (3 marks)

duplicates.reason: Both part a) answers are pseudocode for a conditional over a list, and both part b) answers are a short pseudocode loop. Candidates can reuse the same structure twice for 18 marks.
Both begin by naming a problem-solving strategy and then asking for its application to a supplied scenario. The second is largely a re-test of the first.
The Fibonacci sequence is the subject of a Part A flowchart and again of a Part B recursive program, so one topic carries 12 marks.

summary.headline: 4 questions sit outside the scope you declared, and 31 in-scope topics earn no marks.
strengths: Every question carries a printed CO tag, so the paper is well traced to its outcomes.
The Part A / Part B split matches the 2024-scheme pattern exactly: 8 x 3 plus 4 x 9, with either/or choices only in Part B.
Scenario-based framing in Part B gives candidates a realistic context rather than a bare recall prompt.
risks: Questions 7, 8, 15, 16 assess Module 4, which you declared out of scope, so they will be unanswerable for a class taught only Modules 1-3.
31 in-scope topics, including recursion on the call stack and modularization, carry no marks at all, so strong candidates get no credit for knowing them.
Question 11 a) prints overlapping grade bands (60-70 and 50-69), which will make marking inconsistent.
Several 3-mark questions ask for three separate outputs or for work that needs far more than three marks of effort.
actions: Either widen the scope to include Module 4, or replace questions 7, 8, 15 and 16 with Module 1-3 questions.
Accept the proposed replacements for questions A2 and B11 a) to remove the two highest-risk ambiguities.
Add one 3-mark question on recursion and the call stack, and one on modularization, to close the largest gaps in Module 3.
Fix the printed grade bands in question 11 a) before the paper goes to print; the overlap is a marking problem, not a wording preference.
